claims.text: In single-phase high-entropy alloys, high hardness and strength are primarily governed by local-lattice-distortion resistance to dislocation motion.
Multi-principal-element mixing creates a heterogeneous atomic landscape that preferentially impedes edge dislocations.
Edge dislocations can be prevalent and control plastic flow in a BCC high-entropy alloy.
NbTaTiZrV0.5 is an equiatomic BCC alloy suitable as an example of the proposed initial state.
The proposed initial alloy has a significant fraction of edge dislocations.
Substitution with an element having markedly different atomic size or electronegativity can systematically modulate lattice distortion while phase and grain size are held constant.
Moderately elevated temperatures thermally activate dislocation mobility and reduce alloy strength.
A high fraction of immobilized or pinned edge dislocations mediates the relationship between lattice distortion and strength.
Nano-twinning may accompany the proposed edge-dislocation mediator in FCC systems.
Random variations in atomic size and bonding caused by multi-element mixing produce significant lattice distortions.
Lattice distortions generate spatially varying local-energy landscapes that hinder edge-dislocation motion.
The impediment of edge-dislocation motion acts as an intrinsic barrier that increases yield strength and hardness.
Increasing lattice distortion by compositional modification will increase hardness and yield strength relative to the baseline alloy.
Increasing lattice distortion will produce a greater fraction and greater immobilization of edge dislocations.
At elevated temperature, lattice-distortion-controlled alloys may exhibit a strength plateau or less pronounced thermal softening.
The mechanism is most relevant to single-phase, chemically disordered alloys undergoing dislocation-mediated plasticity at moderate strain rates.
The mechanism may cease to govern multiphase or nanocrystalline alloys when phase- or boundary-mediated processes dominate.
Short-range chemical ordering or nano-twinning could overwhelm or mask the edge-dislocation-pinning effect.
